strengths: TPV provides a clean, unifying lens (Tr(H_eff C)) that connects heterogeneous perturbation mechanisms (SGD noise, label noise, quantization, pruning) through a shared geometric factor, and the paper is explicit about how this differs from global bias-variance decompositions.

The central empirical finding—that training-set TPV matches test-set TPV even at width 1 and is decoupled from generalization gap—is surprising and interesting, since the theory only guarantees it in the infinite-width NTK regime. The honest observation that Theorem 2.1 is sufficient but not necessary adds credibility.

The regime analysis is unusually careful: the pathological cases in Appendix C.2 (interpolation regimes where TPV stability holds trivially but TPV loses discriminative power, and the large-noise regime of Fig. 7 where stability breaks) are thoroughly worked through and reported rather than hidden.

The paper transparently documents practical difficulties (CG non-convergence on ill-conditioned Jacobians, ImageNet fine-tuning failures, discarding runs violating the first-order assumption), which supports reproducibility; experimental details in Appendices F.1-F.3 are extensive.

The JBR pruning criterion is properly positioned as a label-free variant of the Jacobian Criterion with a precise characterization of when the two coincide, and is evaluated under a controlled protocol (same dependency framework, granularity, and schedule) so accuracy differences are attributable to the scoring criterion.
weaknesses: The theoretical core is technically modest. Theorem 2.1 is essentially a triangle-inequality combination of two known ingredients (NTK stability from Jacot et al./Allen-Zhu et al. and an LLN concentration argument), and the proof adds little beyond standard operator-norm bounding. Theorems 3.2 and 3.3 are standard linearization plus Lyapunov/OU arguments (the latter closely follows known SGD noise-covariance results the authors themselves cite, e.g., Wu et al. 2022, Mandt et al. 2017).

There is a significant unexplained gap between theory and empirics: the headline empirical claim (TPV stability at width 1) lies entirely outside the paper's theoretical regime, and the paper offers no explanation for why stability holds at tiny widths. The most interesting phenomenon in the paper is thus unanalyzed.

The empirical TPV protocol may be biased toward confirming the central claim. Runs are discarded if they violate the first-order approximation (checked via finite differences) or if the noisy-model loss does not decrease, which filters out exactly the cases where stability might fail; the paper does not report how many runs were discarded or how sensitive conclusions are to this filtering.

The 'TPV correlates with clean test loss' claim (contribution 3) is under-evidenced: in most experiments (Figs. 5-8, 13) TPV and test loss co-vary with width, so the observed correlation is largely confounded by the width sweep, and the ImageNet evidence (Fig. 6) spans only seven architectures with no statistical analysis.

JBR is an incremental contribution: it differs from the Jacobian Criterion (Chen et al., 2025) only in replacing ground-truth labels with predicted-class one-hot vectors for confident samples, and the reported gains over Jacobian are marginal in several settings (Figs. 9-10, 15-16), making the practical utility claim ('matches or exceeds state-of-the-art') somewhat overstated.

Presentation issues reduce polish: inconsistent references (Mandt et al. cited as 2016/2017; Keskar '& et al.'), typos ('is was extremely difficult', 'Validate Accuracy'), axis label glitches in figures, and an occasionally overclaiming tone ('first result', 'first expression') given prior appearances of the Tr(HC) object in SGD analyses (Zhu et al., 2018; Thomas et al., 2020; Bar et al., 2024).

The stability theorem concerns only the trace-form TPV (Eq. 6), while the main stability experiments use the raw form (Eq. 2); the paper acknowledges this distinction only in a footnote, so the theory provides at best indirect support for the headline experiments.

strengths: The paper proposes a unifying perspective: local prediction variance under parameter perturbations around a trained solution, expressed in trace form Tr(H_eff C), which cleanly separates the geometry of a trained model from the perturbation mechanism (SGD noise, label noise, quantization, pruning). This framing is conceptually appealing and connects several previously separate threads.

The empirical program is broad and careful: 324 synthetic configurations spanning five orders of magnitude in TPV, plus CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet experiments, with a finite-difference first-order validity check and discarding runs that violate the linearization regime. The finding that train-set TPV tracks test-set TPV even at width 1, while breaking at small n_train, is an interesting empirical regularity.

The paper is unusually honest about its limitations: Appendix C.2 systematically analyzes pathological/degenerate regimes (interpolation collapses TPV to a constant; large noise breaks stability), and Appendix C.3 candidly documents that the exact linearized TPV is numerically intractable for modern architectures and describes the practical perturb-and-retrain workaround.

The proofs that are provided (Appendices A, B, C) are correct given their stated assumptions, and the ridge vs. interpolation regime analysis in Appendix C.2 clarifies why TPV retains discriminative power in the small-noise regime.
The JBR pruning criterion is positioned transparently as a label-free variant of the Jacobian Criterion (Chen et al., 2025), with a clear statement of when the two coincide.
weaknesses: The main theoretical contribution (Theorem 2.1, TPV trace stability) is technically shallow. Its proof is essentially a triangle-inequality combination of two known facts (NTK stability during training; LLN concentration of Jacobian second moments at initialization). The 'first result' claim feels overstated: at its core this says two empirical averages of the same population quantity concentrate to the same limit.

There is a significant theory-practice disconnect. The theorem requires infinite-width NTK stability, yet the experiments show stability holds at width 1, and the authors themselves conclude Theorem 2.1 'may not be necessary.' The theory therefore does not explain the central empirical phenomenon. Moreover, the main text theory uses Eq. 6 (trace form) while the stability experiments use Eq. 2 (empirical form), further weakening the link between the stated theorem and the reported results.

The practical relevance of the bound is questionable: the upper bound scales with Tr(C), which for parameter-space perturbations can be enormous, and the NTK error term is only asymptotic in width. No finite-width analysis or non-asymptotic constants are provided.

Theorem 3.2 assumes the perturbation δw is the minimum-norm stationary point of the linearized least-squares problem, but the authors admit SGD does not find this solution in practice (Section 3.1, Appendix C.2); the actual experiments instead use a ridge-regularized perturb-and-retrain procedure that does not match the theorem's assumptions. The derived spectral expression (Eq. 10) thus has an unclear relationship to the measured quantity.

Theorem 3.3 (SGD noise) stacks multiple approximations (dropping the 1/n^2 term, i.i.d. residual assumptions, residual-geometry independence, neglecting O(η^2) terms), and the paper itself notes that gradient-covariance/curvature proportionality is well established in prior work; the increment over known results is modest.

The claimed novelty over prior work is limited. The authors acknowledge that variants of Tr(H_eff C) already appear in analyses of SGD dynamics (Zhu et al., 2018; Thomas et al., 2020; Bar et al., 2024) and that the linear label-noise result is exactly the known Bartlett et al. (2020) expression. The conceptual reframing as a 'variance functional' is a contribution of presentation more than of new understanding.

The JBR pruning contribution is thin: the paper concedes that JBR is essentially a label-free version of the Jacobian Criterion and that the two are identical in the clean, fully-correct-prediction setting. The pruning experiments confirm JBR ≈ Jacobian across all four settings, so the practical takeaway is mostly that a known method works without labels—already expected from the analysis in Chen et al. (2025).

The 'TPV correlates with clean test loss' claim is supported only qualitatively. No correlation coefficients, no comparison against obvious competing metrics (Fisher information trace, Jacobian norm, sharpness measures), which are known to also correlate with generalization. Without such baselines it is impossible to judge whether TPV offers added predictive value.

The core modeling step—treating heterogeneous mechanisms (label noise at convergence, quantization, pruning masks) as small zero-mean Gaussian-like parameter perturbations—is asserted rather than justified, and is clearly inaccurate for pruning (binary masks are not zero-mean perturbations of retained weights). The framework's unification is therefore partly nominal.

Figures 1–4 present '50% error bands' as the stability criterion, which is a loose standard; several points visibly fall outside the band even in the regimes claimed to be stable (e.g., Fig. 2 at n_train=10 is described as broken, but Fig. 4 claims n_train=10 is 'mostly within' the band), making the boundary of the stability claim somewhat inconsistent across sections.

strengths: The paper proposes a clean, unifying quantity (TPV = Tr(H_eff C)) that connects heterogeneous perturbation sources (label noise, SGD noise, quantization, pruning) through a common curvature–covariance interaction, and clearly distinguishes this local notion from global prediction variance studied in prior bias–variance work.

The empirical TPV stability observation is genuinely striking: TPV_train ≈ TPV_test across 324 synthetic configurations spanning five orders of magnitude and across CIFAR-10/100 architectures, including surprisingly narrow (width=1) networks. The experimental hygiene is good—first-order validity checks via finite differences, controlled mini-batch ordering, eval-mode training to isolate label noise.

The analysis of pathological regimes (Appendix C.2) is unusually thorough and honest: the authors carefully delineate interpolation regimes where TPV stability holds trivially but TPV loses discriminative power, and regimes where stability genuinely breaks, and they acknowledge that their Theorem 2.1 may be sufficient but not necessary.

The pruning application (JBR) is competitive with strong baselines including the Jacobian Criterion across four standard settings, demonstrating practical utility of the framework, and the relationship to JC is analyzed explicitly rather than hidden.
The derivation of label-noise TPV for finite-width networks (Theorem 3.2, Eq. 10) is a nice spectral characterization, and the connection to benign overfitting via NTK conditioning is well-motivated.
weaknesses: The theoretical novelty is modest. The trace stability theorem (Thm 2.1 / A.4) is essentially a combination of standard NTK stability and a law-of-large-numbers argument, and the resulting bound scales with Tr(C), making it loose precisely in the regimes the authors care about (large perturbations). Theorem 3.3 (TPV_SGD ∝ ησ²/(2b) Tr(Hessian)) and Remark 3.4 are well-known results in the SGD-noise/flat-minima literature, as the authors themselves acknowledge in Appendix D.1. Theorem 3.2's linear case is explicitly the Bartlett et al. (2020) result. The contribution is thus largely reframing and interpretation rather than new mathematics.

There is a significant theory–practice gap that the paper acknowledges but does not resolve: the theorem requires extreme overparameterization (NTK regime, m→∞), yet the headline empirical finding is that stability holds even at width=1. This means the proof does not explain the central empirical phenomenon, weakening the significance of the theoretical contribution.

The claimed correlation between TPV and test loss is demonstrated mainly by varying width as a single knob (Figures 5–8). Since width changes both test loss and Jacobian conditioning simultaneously, the correlation could be confounded by width rather than reflecting a genuine TPV–generalization link; evidence across independent model families is limited to one ImageNet scatter plot (Fig. 6) with seven points.

JBR's novelty over the Jacobian Criterion (Chen et al., 2025) is thin—it is a label-free variant differing only in the logit-space vector m(x), and the pruning figures show JBR and Jacobian curves nearly overlapping. 'Matches or exceeds' appears to mostly mean 'matches'.

Several promised perturbation sources are not empirically studied: no SGD-noise TPV or quantization TPV experiments are included (deferred to prior work), so the 'unifying lens' claim is validated for only label noise and pruning in practice. The ImageNet TPV experiments also appear fragile (training loss could not be driven down for several architectures, requiring shuffling workarounds).

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned despite the substantial experimental pipeline (Monte Carlo retraining loops, Jacobian SVDs, pruning framework built on OBC), and some hyperparameters (e.g., the τ=0.9 confidence threshold, proximity regularization γ) are stated without sensitivity analysis.

strengths: The paper proposes a genuinely unifying lens: the decomposition TPV = Tr(H_eff C) cleanly separates the label-free geometric factor (output-parameter Jacobian second moment) from the perturbation mechanism encoded in C, and the authors show this same trace form covers label noise, SGD stationary noise, quantization noise, and pruning masks.

Theoretical results are meaningful: Theorem 3.1 (TPV trace stability) provides the first formal justification for using training-set TPV as a proxy for test-set TPV; Theorem 4.2 extends benign overfitting intuition from linear models (where it exactly recovers Bartlett et al. 2020) to nonlinear networks via Jacobian spectral geometry; Theorem 4.3 connects SGD noise TPV to the wide-minima hypothesis and clarifies why training-set sharpness can even anti-correlate with label-noise sensitivity (Appendix I.4).

Empirical verification is broad and mostly convincing: over 300 synthetic configurations plus CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, ResNet-18 training trajectories, and BERT NLU fine-tuning, consistently demonstrating that train/test TPV stability holds far beyond the NTK/isotropic assumptions of the theory, including at width 1.

Applications are practically relevant: training-set-only model selection across recipes, architectures, and transfer settings (Figs. 9-11, 25), and the argmax-TPV epoch landmark identifying the double-descent transition along a single training run without validation labels.

The paper is unusually honest about limitations: the pathological-regime analysis in Appendix D.2 (interpolation degeneracy, large-noise breakdown, CG non-convergence due to ill-conditioning) is thorough and candid, and the impact statement correctly scopes the theory's assumptions.
weaknesses: The theoretical novelty is modest. Theorem 3.1 is a fairly direct combination of known NTK stability (Jacot et al.; Allen-Zhu et al.) with the law of large numbers under a strong isotropic-covariance assumption (A.3); the linear-case result is exactly the known benign-overfitting expression; the SGD-noise Hessian proportionality is acknowledged to be known in related forms (Mandt et al., Wu et al., Mori). The unification is largely conceptual repackaging rather than new machinery.

The headline pruning application (JBR) is very close to the existing Jacobiab Criterion (JC, Chen et al. 2025) - the paper itself shows the two differ only in the choice of logit-space vector (p(x) - e_c(x) vs. p(x) - y(x)) and are equivalent when the model fits training labels. Claiming 'matching state-of-the-art baselines' for a one-vector-substitution variant is incremental.

There is a gap between the theoretical object and the empirical estimator: the practical TPV estimate requires R = 5-50 full fine-tuning runs per evaluated model, with several ad hoc heuristics (adaptive noise scaling c, eval-mode training, fixed data-loader seeds, discarding non-converged runs via a finite-difference check). The computational cost of this protocol is never quantified, which weakens the practical model-selection claims, and it is unclear how much the empirical quantity still reflects Tr(H_eff C).

Some key claims rest on empirical correlation rather than theory: the U-shaped TPV-vs-test-loss relationship and the model-selection utility are observed phenomena without predictive theory, and the correlation is acknowledged to be noisy within regularization groups and weak across architectures (Fig. 25), limiting the generality of the training-set-only selection claim.

The stability theorem gives only an upper bound with loose constants (scaling with p and Tr(C)), and the appendix discussion of when the bound is vacuous is largely qualitative; the claimed 'first theoretical result' framing slightly overstates the strength of what is proved.

Presentation issues: Figure 1 conflates two perturbation sources in one scatter with heavy visual density; several proofs (e.g., the Lyapunov-equation derivation in Appendix E) rely on informal approximations (dropping 1/n^2 terms, O(eta) neglect) that are stated rather than rigorously controlled.

strengths: The central trace identity TPV ≈ Tr(H_eff C) is a clean, unifying object, and the paper is diligent in connecting it to several known lines of work (benign overfitting via Eq. 9 matching Bartlett et al., SGD noise via Hessian proportionality, quantization noise), which makes the framework conceptually tidy.

The empirical program is extensive: 324 synthetic configurations, CIFAR-10/100 with multiple architectures and widths, ImageNet, transfer learning on Oxford Pets, and BERT NLU runs, with a useful empirical finding that train/test TPV stability holds far beyond the NTK/isotropic assumptions of the theorem.

The paper is unusually honest about limitations: Appendix D.2 analyzes degenerate interpolation regimes where TPV becomes uninformative, D.3.3 documents that exact linearized TPV is numerically intractable for deep networks, and the impact statement acknowledges the scope of the theoretical guarantees.

The application experiments (JBR pruning against 7 baselines on OBC protocol; four model-selection scenarios without test labels) demonstrate that the framework can produce usable practical tools, and Fig. 11's sharpness-sign-inversion analysis is an interesting observation connecting to the flatness debate.
The appendix contains detailed reproducibility information (full hyperparameters, seeds, protocols for disabling shuffle/eval-mode subtleties), which exceeds typical practice.
weaknesses: The core mathematical object is technically thin: Eq. 1/6 is a one-line first-order Taylor expansion, and H_eff is just the Gauss-Newton/Fisher second moment. Framing this well-known decomposition as a new 'unifying lens' overstates originality; the pieces (Tr(HC) appearing in Zhu et al., Bar et al., Thomas et al.) are acknowledged but the added value beyond relabeling is modest.

Theorem 3.1 (the central 'first theoretical result' claim) is weak: it requires isotropic perturbation covariance C = σ²I_p, which contradicts every covariance the paper itself derives (label-noise C = σ²X^T(XX^T)^{-2}X, pruning C block-diagonal, quantization only isotropic by assumption). The result also only holds as m → ∞ with ε_NTK → 0 and n_tr, n_te → ∞ — a regime where train/test agreement is essentially the LLN and nearly trivial. The theorem therefore provides little support for the empirical stability observed at width = 1 and anisotropic noise, i.e., the gap between theory and the empirics the paper emphasizes is large.

Theorem 4.2's connection to actual SGD solutions is heuristic: it characterizes the minimum-norm stationary point of the linearized loss, but the paper provides no proof that SGD on the true nonlinear objective reaches this point; the empirical agreement in Figs. 4-5 partially compensates but the 'first expression for finite-width networks' claim rests on this unverified approximation.

Theorem 4.3 is labeled a theorem but relies on two informal approximations (dropping rank-1 term, iid residuals independent of Jacobian geometry), neglecting O(η²) terms, and assumes H_eff ≈ Hessian at small residuals — this is a heuristic derivation, not a theorem.

The headline stability result is also somewhat expected: on i.i.d. data, empirical second moments of Jacobians on train vs. test sets concentrate by the law of large numbers, so Fig. 1's diagonal is unsurprising; the surprising width=1 result is exactly the case the theorem does not cover and no theory explains it.

Practical significance of the label-free model selection is questionable: each TPV estimate requires R = 5-50 full fine-tuning runs of the reference model on noisy logits. For many deployment scenarios, simply holding out a small validation set would be cheaper and more reliable; the paper does not report compute cost comparisons against this baseline.

JBR is a very minor variant of the Jacobian Criterion (the only difference is m_JC(x) = p(x) − y vs. m_JBR(x) = p(x) − e_{c(x)}, identical when labels and predictions are clean); presenting it as a distinct state-of-the-art-matching criterion overstates the delta.

Internal inconsistencies suggest insufficient polish: the appendix references a 'Theorem 2.1' that does not exist in the main text, Theorem 3.1's bound scales with p but the theorem statement in the main text drops this factor into c₁, and the equivalence to Barlett et al. requires assumptions (whitened features, θ* in row span) that make the 'extension to nonlinear networks' connection looser than presented.

The link between TPV and generalization is fundamentally correlational: the decomposition Eq. 3 holds only for squared loss, yet the paper correlates TPV with cross-entropy test loss throughout, an empirical relationship with no theoretical grounding and acknowledged noisiness (Fig. 18).

strengths: The paper presents a clean, unifying framework: the trace form Tr(H_eff C) separates model geometry from perturbation mechanism, and the paper convincingly shows that SGD noise, label noise, quantization, and pruning can all be analyzed through this single lens, connecting previously disparate threads (wide minima, benign overfitting, NTK).

The theoretical derivations are correct and carefully done: the trace stability proof (Appendix A) is elementary but sound under its stated assumptions; the label-noise TPV derivation (Appendix D) is clean, correctly recovers Bartlett et al. (2020) benign overfitting as a special case, and Theorem 4.2 makes no interpolation assumption, which the authors clarify precisely in the regime analysis of Appendix D.2.

The empirical work is unusually broad and honest: 324 synthetic configurations spanning five orders of magnitude in TPV, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, BERT NLU experiments, and four deployment scenarios. The findings that TPV stability holds even at width=1 and is decoupled from the generalization gap are genuinely surprising and well-documented.

The authors are refreshingly candid about limitations: they document the failure of exact linearized TPV computation on deep networks (Appendix D.3.3), the regimes where TPV stability breaks or becomes trivial (D.2), the weakening of cross-architecture model selection (Appendix I.3), and the sharpness sign-inversion analysis (Appendix I.4) that explains rather than hides an inconvenient result.

The practical payoff (training-set-only model selection and the JBR pruning criterion) is grounded in the framework rather than bolted on, and JBR's relationship to the Jacobian Criterion is analyzed precisely (Appendix H.1), identifying the exact condition under which the two coincide.

Reproducibility is strong: hyperparameters, seeds, protocols (eval mode, fixed mini-batch order, noise scaling) and model sources are all specified in extensive appendices, and the impact statement is appropriate.
weaknesses: The central theorem (TPV Trace Stability) is a modest result technically: it follows from a triangle-inequality decomposition combining NTK stability and the LLN, and requires a strong isotropic-perturbation assumption (C = σ²I_p) that is far from the realistic perturbations (anisotropic SGD noise, structured label noise) the paper emphasizes. The gap between what the theorem guarantees and the far broader empirical stability (including width=1, far outside the NTK regime) remains unexplained and is explicitly left as future work.

The claimed 'first result' that prediction variance under parameter perturbations can be inferred from training inputs alone is somewhat overclaimed: training-set NTK trace concentration follows fairly directly from known NTK stability and Jacobian concentration results, and the trace form itself is acknowledged to appear in prior work (Zhu et al., 2018; Thomas et al., 2020; Bar et al., 2024).

The practical label-noise TPV estimator (perturb-and-retrain, Appendix D.3.4) is a heuristic that does not compute the min-norm linearized solution analyzed in Theorem 4.2; the link between the estimator and the theory is qualitative, and the reported 'Theory vs Empirical' agreement is only verified on small synthetic MLPs where exact SVD is feasible.

The TPV–test-loss relationship is explicitly an empirical, U-shaped, regime-dependent observation (positive in the low training loss regime, inverted under underfitting), which limits the reliability of the model-selection application: it is strongest only within-architecture and requires the practitioner to know they are in the low training loss regime. Cross-architecture selection is admittedly weaker.

JBR is a small delta over the Jacobian Criterion of Chen et al. (2025) — the two differ only in the logit-space vector m(x) — and the paper itself notes the TPV trace stability theorem does not strictly apply to the functional u(·) used for pruning, so the pruning contribution is largely an empirical one.

Minor presentation issues undermine polish: dangling references to a non-existent 'Theorem 2.1' (Appendix D.2 summary and page 5 text reference Theorem 3.1 inconsistently), and the main-text Theorem 3.1 is actually proven as Theorem A.5 with a slightly different constant presentation.

The theorem's bound involves Tr(C), which grows with parameter count p, so the bound can be vacuous for realistic noise scales in large networks; the paper does not discuss the tightness of the bound quantitatively.
